title: Lewis v. State
description: Whether venue for felony murder charges, where the predicate drug sale occurs in one county and the death in another, should be determined by the location of the drug sale or the location of the death.
plaintiff_argument: Lewis argued that venue was not proper in Gwinnett County because the predicate felony (drug sale) occurred in DeKalb County, and there was no allegation of his actions establishing venue in Gwinnett.
defendant_argument: The State argued that venue was proper in Gwinnett County because it was the location where the cause of death, the ingestion of narcotics, and the res gestae of Lewis's actions resulted.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the trial court's order denying Lewis's amended motion to dismiss and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.

title: Guy v. Hous. Authority of Augusta
description: Whether a local housing authority, authorized by state statute but activated by city government, is protected from a personal injury suit by sovereign immunity.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Christina Guy, argued that the Housing Authority of the City of Augusta was negligent in providing safety and security, implying it is not protected by sovereign immunity and can be sued.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Housing Authority of the City of Augusta, argued that it is protected by sovereign immunity as an instrumentality of the State, a municipal corporation, or an instrumentality of a municipality, and therefore the personal injury suit should be dismissed.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals' judgment and remanded the case for further consideration of the housing authority's immunity under the proper common law analytical approach.

title: Bailey v. McKintosh County, Webster v. McIntosh County, McIntosh County v. Webster
description: Whether a zoning ordinance passed by McIntosh County, which increased the allowable maximum dwelling size in a historic district, is subject to a citizen-initiated referendum under the Georgia Constitution's Home Rule Provision, with the plaintiff arguing it is not subject to such a referendum and the defendant arguing it is.
plaintiff_argument: McIntosh County argued that its zoning ordinance was passed under the Zoning Provision of the Georgia Constitution, not the Home Rule Provision, and therefore is not subject to the referendum process.
defendant_argument: The Intervenors and Judge Webster argued that the superior court erred in concluding that the zoning ordinance was not subject to the referendum procedures of the Home Rule Provision, asserting that the Home Rule Provision does apply to zoning ordinances.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the superior court's order that halted the referendum and issued a writ of prohibition against Judge Webster, concluding that the zoning ordinance is subject to the Home Rule Provision's referendum procedures. The Court affirmed the superior court's injunction preventing enforcement of the Ordinance pending appeal.

title: Stephens v. State
description: Whether OCGA § 16-11-126 (g) (1), which prohibits 18- to 20-year-olds from carrying handguns in public, violates Article I, Section I, Paragraph VIII of the Georgia Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Thomas Stephens, argued that the state statute prohibiting 18- to 20-year-olds from carrying handguns in public violates the Georgia Constitution's right to bear arms and requested the court to overrule its long-standing precedent.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State of Georgia, argued that the age restriction is a reasonable safety measure, not arbitrary, and not a complete prohibition on the right to bear arms, thus constituting a permissible exercise of police power.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, ruling against Stephens's constitutional challenge to the state statute prohibiting 18- to 20-year-olds from carrying handguns in public.

title: State v. Dias
description: Whether evidence of a defendant's refusal to submit to a warrantless blood test for DUI can be admitted at trial without violating constitutional rights, with the State arguing it can and Dias arguing it cannot.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that admitting blood-test refusal evidence does not violate the Fourth or Fifth Amendments or the Georgia Constitution's self-incrimination and search/seizure provisions.
defendant_argument: Dias argues that admitting evidence of her refusal to a warrantless blood test violates her Fourth Amendment rights against unreasonable searches and seizures, her Fifth Amendment due process rights, and her Georgia constitutional rights against self-incrimination.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the trial court's judgment that excluded the blood-test refusal evidence and remanded the case for consideration of other potential grounds for exclusion.

title: Republican National Committee v. Eternal Vigilance Action, Inc; Georgia v. Eternal Vigilance Action
description: Whether the Georgia General Assembly can delegate broad rulemaking authority over elections to the State Elections Board (SEB) without sufficient guidelines, and whether various plaintiffs have standing to challenge these rules.
plaintiff_argument: The SEB rules are unconstitutional and unauthorized by the Election Code, violating the nondelegation doctrine and infringing on the fundamental right to vote, and the plaintiffs have standing to challenge them based on organizational, associational, community-stakeholder, or individual voter rights.
defendant_argument: The SEB rules are constitutional and authorized by the General Assembly with sufficient guidelines, the plaintiffs lack standing to challenge them, and their claims are too vague for declaratory relief.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part, reversed in part, and vacated and remanded in part. It ruled that organizational plaintiffs lacked standing, but individual plaintiffs had standing to challenge five of the seven rules. Four of these five rules (Reasonable Inquiry, Examination, Hand Count, Drop Box ID) were found invalid due to unauthorized delegation of legislative power, while the Drop Box Surveillance Rule was upheld. The trial court's finding on Hall's standing as an election board member was vacated and remanded for further consideration. The trial court's finding that SEB rules violated the Federal Elections Clause was reversed.

title: Atlantic Games, Inc. v. Georgia Lottery Corporation
description: Whether the General Assembly's delegation of rulemaking authority to the Georgia Lottery Corporation violated the nondelegation doctrine due to a lack of clear statutory guidance.
plaintiff_argument: Atlantic Games argues that the General Assembly's delegation of rulemaking authority to the Georgia Lottery Corporation lacked clear statutory guidance, violating the Georgia nondelegation doctrine, and asked the court to reconsider a previous decision.
defendant_argument: The defendant implicitly argues that the delegation of rulemaking authority was permissible and did not violate the nondelegation doctrine.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court denied the petition for certiorari in this case, allowing the lower court's decision to stand.

title: White v. City of Mableton
description: Whether House Bill 839 violates the Single Subject Rule of the Georgia Constitution by creating both the City of Mableton and Community Improvement Districts within the same legislative act.
plaintiff_argument: HB 839 is unconstitutional because it creates "more than one unit of government" (Mableton and CIDs) in a single act, violating the Single Subject Rule and the precedent set in Rea v. City of LaFayette.
defendant_argument: HB 839 does not violate the Single Subject Rule or Rea because the creation of CIDs is logically connected and germane to the incorporation of Mableton.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's dismissal of the Appellants' complaint, ruling that HB 839 does not violate the Single Subject Rule or run afoul of Rea.

title: Wasserman v. Franklin County
description: Whether the federal doctrine of third-party standing survives as a means of obtaining standing in Georgia courts.
plaintiff_argument: Wasserman argued that she had standing under the federal doctrine of third-party standing, that Georgia's standing requirements were unconstitutional or preempted for her federal claim, and that Pham assigned his rights to her.
defendant_argument: Franklin County argued that Wasserman lacked standing to assert Pham's equal protection rights.
decision_outcome: The court overruled the precedent that adopted the federal doctrine of third-party standing, concluding that a plaintiff must assert their own legal rights to maintain an action in Georgia courts, and vacated and remanded the lower court's judgment.

title: Sumrall v. State
description: Whether OCGA § 42-8-66 (a) (1) unconstitutionally restricts access to the courts and the right to prosecute and defend one's cause, and whether the trial court erred in dismissing Sumrall's petition for retroactive first-offender treatment due to lack of prosecuting attorney consent.
plaintiff_argument: Sumrall argued that OCGA § 42-8-66 (a) (1) is unconstitutional as it restricts his access to the courts and right to prosecute and defend his cause, and that the prosecuting attorney's inaction constituted implied consent to his petition.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the statute is constitutional, Sumrall failed to obtain the required prosecutorial consent, and therefore the trial court properly dismissed his petition without a hearing.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the trial court's dismissal of Sumrall's petition for retroactive first-offender treatment and the denial of his motion to declare OCGA § 42-8-66 (a) (1) unconstitutional.

title: Hollis v. City of LaGrange
description: Whether the City of LaGrange's excessive utility charges constitute illegal taxes not authorized by the Georgia Constitution or law, and whether the trial court has the authority to review such claims.
plaintiff_argument: The City's excessive utility charges are illegal taxes because they generate profits beyond the cost of services, used for general revenue, and are not expressly authorized by the Georgia Constitution or law. The trial court has the authority to review these claims.
defendant_argument: The trial court is not authorized to regulate municipal public utilities charges because the Georgia Constitution prohibits the General Assembly from regulating or fixing such charges, and courts cannot do what the General Assembly cannot do.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the trial court's judgment, ruling that the trial court erred in concluding it lacked authority to review the plaintiffs' legal claims, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Gonzalez v. Miller
description: Whether the Open Records Act (ORA) applies to district attorneys' offices and whether prosecutorial immunity bars enforcement actions against them, with the plaintiff arguing that the ORA applies and his lawsuit should proceed, and the defendant arguing that her office is not subject to the ORA and she is protected by prosecutorial immunity.
plaintiff_argument: Miller argued that District Attorney Gonzalez violated the Open Records Act (ORA) by failing to produce requested public records and destroying correspondence, and that her office is subject to the ORA, allowing his enforcement action to proceed.
defendant_argument: Gonzalez contended that neither she nor her office is subject to the ORA because district attorneys are constitutional officers of the judicial branch, that Miller lacks standing, and that prosecutorial immunity bars his suit.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's denial of Gonzalez's motion to dismiss, holding that the Open Records Act applies to district attorneys' offices, Miller has constitutional standing, and prosecutorial immunity does not bar official-capacity claims, thus allowing Miller's lawsuit to proceed.

title: Satcher v. Columbia County
description: Whether the permanent injunction granted against Columbia County for stormwater drainage issues was barred by sovereign immunity, and whether property owners could recover damages incurred after providing notice to the county.
plaintiff_argument: The property owners argued they were entitled to a permanent injunction and damages for the county's continuing nuisance and inverse condemnation, including damages incurred after providing notice.
defendant_argument: Columbia County argued that sovereign immunity barred the permanent injunction and that the property owners could not recover damages incurred after notice under OCGA § 36-11-1.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals's opinion regarding the injunction, ruling that the trial court's permanent injunction exceeded the scope of sovereign immunity waiver, and also vacated the grant of certiorari for the property owners' damages petition, effectively denying it.

title: Williams v. Powell
description: Whether OCGA § 16-11-34.1 (a), (f), and (g), which criminalize conduct disrupting legislative meetings, are unconstitutionally overbroad or vague under the Georgia Constitution's free speech protections.
plaintiff_argument: The appellants argued that OCGA § 16-11-34.1 (a), (f), and (g) are unconstitutionally overbroad and vague, violating free speech protections, and that the trial court erred in dismissing their facial and as-applied challenges.
defendant_argument: The appellees argued that OCGA § 16-11-34.1 is not facially unconstitutional, not unconstitutionally vague, and that the specific as-applied claim (Cannon's) failed to show protected expression, distinguishing it from a previously invalidated statute.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, rejecting the appellants' facial challenges to OCGA § 16-11-34.1 (a), (f), and (g) as unconstitutionally overbroad or vague, and rejecting one appellant's as-applied challenge.

title: Cobb County v. Floam
description: Whether the Floams were entitled to declaratory relief regarding the constitutionality of the Cobb County Board of Commissioners' amendment changing commission district boundaries, with the Floams arguing they faced uncertainty warranting such relief and Cobb County arguing they did not.
plaintiff_argument: The Floams argued that the Cobb County Board of Commissioners' amendment changing district boundaries was unconstitutional, and they sought a declaratory judgment because they faced uncertainty regarding their voting rights and district representation, which constituted an individualized injury.
defendant_argument: Cobb County argued that the Floams lacked constitutional standing because they did not allege an individualized injury, and even if they had standing, they did not demonstrate the requisite uncertainty about future decisions to warrant declaratory relief.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's decision, concluding that while the Floams had constitutional standing as community stakeholders, they did not show the necessary uncertainty about their future conduct to obtain declaratory relief, and therefore their claim must be dismissed without reaching the merits of the constitutional arguments.

title: Lovell v. Raffensperger
description: Whether actions seeking declaratory and injunctive relief against state or local government actors must be brought exclusively against the state or relevant local government and in their name, as required by Paragraph V of the Georgia Constitution, to waive sovereign immunity.
plaintiff_argument: Appellants argued that the superior courts erred in dismissing their claims, contending that Paragraph V's waiver of sovereign immunity applied to their actions seeking declaratory relief from acts of the state.
defendant_argument: The trial courts (and implicitly the defendants) argued that the actions were barred by sovereign immunity because the appellants failed to comply with Paragraph V by not naming the State of Georgia or the relevant local governments as the exclusive defendants and in their name.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the superior courts' dismissal of the actions, concluding that the appellants failed to comply with Paragraph V (b) (2) of the Georgia Constitution.

title: In Re: Prosecuting Attorneys Qualifications Commission Rules and Code of Conduct
description: Whether the Supreme Court of Georgia has the constitutional power to adopt the draft standards of conduct and rules for the Prosecuting Attorneys Qualifications Commission.
plaintiff_argument: The Prosecuting Attorneys Qualifications Commission transmitted draft standards and rules for the Court's review and adoption, implicitly seeking the Court's approval and suggesting it has the power to do so.
defendant_argument: The Supreme Court expressed grave doubts about its constitutional power to adopt the standards and rules, citing separation of powers and the nature of judicial versus executive power exercised by district attorneys.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court respectfully declined to take any action regarding the Commission's draft standards of conduct and rules for its governance.

title: Roberts v. Cuthpert
description: Whether a probate judge is immune from claims for costs and attorney's fees after wrongly denying a weapons carry license, and whether such recovery violates the Separation of Powers Provision of the Georgia Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the General Assembly waived sovereign immunity for claims under OCGA § 16-11-129 (j), that the probate judge waived judicial immunity, and that the recovery of costs and attorney's fees does not violate the Separation of Powers Provision because processing a weapons carry license is not a judicial function.
defendant_argument: The defendant probate judges argued that judicial immunity and sovereign immunity barred the costs-and-fees claim, and that the recovery of costs and attorney's fees was unconstitutional under the Separation of Powers Provision, implying the function was judicial.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part, ruling that sovereign immunity was waived, judicial immunity was waived by the judge, and the recovery of costs and attorney's fees does not violate the Separation of Powers Provision because granting/denying a weapons carry license is a nonjudicial function. The case was remanded for a hearing on costs and attorney's fees.

title: Raffensperger v. Jackson
description: Whether the Georgia Lactation Consultant Practice Act violates due process rights by unreasonably restricting individuals from practicing their chosen profession as lactation care providers.
plaintiff_argument: The Act is irrational and lacks a real connection to public health, safety, or welfare, forcing them to cease practicing their profession and violating their due process and equal protection rights.
defendant_argument: The Act does not prevent plaintiffs from practicing their profession and is rationally related to protecting public health, safety, and welfare by ensuring access to quality care.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's decision, ruling that the Georgia Lactation Consultant Practice Act is unconstitutional as it violates the plaintiffs' due process rights to practice their chosen profession.

title: In re Judge Christian Coomer
description: Whether the Judicial Qualifications Commission (JQC) has jurisdiction over a judge's conduct that occurred before they became a judge or judicial candidate, and whether negligent conduct outside a judicial capacity can warrant discipline.
plaintiff_argument: The JQC Director argued that the JQC has jurisdiction over conduct occurring before a person became a judge or judicial candidate, and that even mere negligence for actions taken outside a judicial capacity could warrant discipline.
defendant_argument: Judge Coomer argued that the JQC lacked jurisdiction over pre-judicial conduct because the Code of Judicial Conduct does not apply to such actions, and that disciplining him for such conduct would violate due process rights. He also contended that the JQC's authority over judicial candidates is limited to campaigning and politics.
decision_outcome: The court remanded the case to the JQC Hearing Panel, ruling that the Code of Judicial Conduct does not apply to pre-judicial conduct and that discipline for non-judicial conduct requires a finding of bad faith, not mere negligence.

title: Session v. State
description: Whether the Georgia sex offender registration statute, as applied to Derrick Session, violates his federal rights to travel and equal protection, or the Georgia Constitution's Social Status Provision, and whether the evidence was insufficient to support his convictions for failure to register.
plaintiff_argument: Derrick Session argued that the evidence was insufficient to support his Georgia convictions, that the Georgia registration statute violated his federal rights to travel and equal protection by treating him differently than a native Georgian for a similar offense, and that it violated the Georgia constitutional prohibition against legislation regarding the social status of citizens.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the evidence was sufficient, Session's federal rights arguments were based on speculative assumptions, and the Georgia registration statute does not violate the Georgia Constitution's Social Status Provision, and that Louisiana's extended registration period did not violate ex post facto principles.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Session's convictions, rejecting all his arguments regarding the insufficiency of evidence and the unconstitutionality of the Georgia sex offender registration statute.

title: Johnson v. State
description: Whether a pro se filing made by a defendant who is actually or presumptively represented by counsel is always a legal nullity.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that such pro se filings should not always be considered legal nullities, as this rule can prevent defendants from preserving their appeal rights.
defendant_argument: The defendant implicitly argues that pro se filings by counseled defendants are legal nullities, based on past precedent, and raises concerns about counsel's ethical obligations if such filings are allowed.
decision_outcome: The court overruled its past decisions that held pro se filings by counseled defendants are always legal nullities, affirming that courts retain discretion to recognize such filings, and vacated the judgment, remanding the case for the trial court to exercise this discretion.

title: Taylor v. The Devereux Foundation
description: Whether the statutory cap on punitive damages (OCGA § 51-12-5.1 (g)) violates the Georgia Constitution's guarantees of the right to trial by jury, separation of powers, and equal protection.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Taylor, argued that the $250,000 cap on punitive damages is unconstitutional because it violates the right to trial by jury, the guarantee of separation of powers, and the guarantee of equal protection under the Georgia Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Devereux, argued that the punitive damages cap is constitutional, contending that Taylor failed to prove the punitive damages sought were within the scope of the 1798 Georgia constitutional right to a jury trial, and that the cap does not violate separation of powers or equal protection.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision to apply the punitive damages cap, reducing Taylor's punitive damages award from $50,000,000 to $250,000, and also affirmed the attorney fees and post-judgment interest rulings.

title: State v. SASS Group
description: Whether the term "action" in Paragraph V of the Georgia Constitution, which waives sovereign immunity for certain suits against the State, refers to an entire lawsuit or only a specific claim within a lawsuit, thereby determining if a suit naming additional defendants must be dismissed in its entirety.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that "action" means a claim or cause of action, not an entire lawsuit, allowing them to include claims against the State (under Paragraph V's waiver) and other defendants in the same lawsuit, with only the Paragraph V-reliant claims needing to comply with exclusivity.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that "action" means the entire case or lawsuit, and therefore, if any claim in a lawsuit relies on Paragraph V's waiver, the entire suit must be brought exclusively against the State or be dismissed.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's denial of the State's motion to dismiss, vacated the interlocutory injunction, and remanded the case with direction that it be dismissed.

title: Camden County v. Sweatt
description: Whether the Home Rule Paragraph of the Georgia Constitution authorizes county electorates to petition for a special election to repeal resolutions adopted by the county's governing authority, with the County arguing it does not and the electors arguing it does.
plaintiff_argument: Camden County argued that the Home Rule Paragraph does not authorize referendums on resolutions adopted by the county's governing authority, limiting such referendums to 'local acts' only.
defendant_argument: Sweatt, et al. (the electors) argued that the Home Rule Paragraph explicitly grants the electorate the power to seek a referendum on the amendment or repeal of 'ordinances, resolutions, or regulations adopted pursuant to subparagraph (a).'
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the superior court's denial of Camden County's petition for declaratory relief, mandamus, and prohibition, thereby upholding the validity of the referendum.

title: Ammons v. State
description: Whether evidence of a defendant's refusal to perform preliminary breath tests and field sobriety tests violates the Georgia Constitution's right against compelled self-incrimination, and whether statutes allowing evidence of refusal to consent to a blood test violate the Georgia Privileges and Immunities Clause.
plaintiff_argument: Ammons argued that using evidence of her refusal to perform breath and field sobriety tests violates her right against self-incrimination, and that statutes permitting evidence of her refusal to consent to a blood test violate the General Assembly's constitutional duty to protect citizens' rights, privileges, and immunities.
defendant_argument: The State argued that evidence of Ammons's refusal to perform tests is admissible and does not violate the Georgia Constitution, relying on prior precedent for preliminary breath tests and asserting that the Privileges and Immunities Clause does not bar admission of blood test refusal evidence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part, ruling that evidence of refusal to perform preliminary breath and field sobriety tests is inadmissible, but evidence of refusal to consent to a blood test is admissible.

title: Reed v. State
description: Whether Jaquavious Reed's conviction for murder and other charges should be overturned due to alleged errors including insufficient evidence, appellate delay, denial of right to be present, prosecutorial conflict, incomplete transcript, Brady violation, denial of continuance, ineffective assistance of counsel, and improper sentencing.
plaintiff_argument: Reed argued his conviction should be overturned due to insufficient evidence, inordinate appellate delay, denial of his right to be present at bench conferences, a conflict of interest with the DA's office, an incomplete trial transcript, a Brady violation, denial of a continuance for a surprise witness, ineffective assistance of counsel, and improper sentencing.
defendant_argument: The State argued the evidence was sufficient, Reed failed to show prejudice from appellate delay or incomplete transcript, his right to be present was not violated or was waived, the conflict of interest claim was waived, there was no Brady violation, and the denial of continuance was not an abuse of discretion, while conceding the improper sentencing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Reed's conviction for malice murder, vacated his conviction for felony murder, and remanded the case for resentencing, denying all other claims for overturning the conviction.

title: Prickett v. State
description: Whether the trial court erred in denying Prickett's motion for a new trial based on claims of ineffective assistance of counsel, violation of his right to be present, and prosecutorial misconduct, and whether Prickett's convictions and sentences should be vacated.
plaintiff_argument: Prickett argued that the trial court erred by denying his motion for a new trial due to ineffective assistance of counsel, violation of his right to be present, and failure to address prosecutorial misconduct, and that his convictions and sentences should be vacated.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the trial court correctly denied the motion for a new trial as there was no prejudice or constitutional violation, and that the convictions were valid.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of Prickett's motion for a new trial but vacated his convictions and sentences, remanding the case for resentencing due to errors in the original sentencing.

title: Awad v. State
description: Whether Paragraph XVI of the Georgia Constitution prohibits the State from admitting into evidence a defendant's refusal to submit to a state-administered urine test for chemical testing, on the grounds that it violates the right against compelled self-incrimination.
plaintiff_argument: Awad argued that the right against compelled self-incrimination protected by Paragraph XVI of the Georgia Constitution prohibits the State from admitting evidence of his refusal to submit to a urine test, as providing a urine sample in a collection container requires an affirmative act that generates self-incriminating evidence.
defendant_argument: The State argued that obtaining a urine sample does not implicate the right against compelled self-incrimination because it does not require an 'act' on the part of the defendant, comparing it to other bodily substances like DNA or blood, and that commenting on refusal does not necessarily implicate rights under Paragraph XVI.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that the trial court properly suppressed evidence of Awad's refusal to submit to a urine test, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Harvey v. Merchan
description: Whether Georgia or Quebec law applies to Merchan's claims, whether OCGA § 9-3-33.1 can revive a cause of action for acts that did not occur in Georgia, and whether Georgia's constitutional ban on retroactive laws and the due process and equal protection clauses of the federal and state constitutions would bar Merchan's pursuit of such a cause of action against her parents.
plaintiff_argument: Merchan argued that Georgia substantive law should apply to all claims, including those for abuse in Quebec, under a 'continuing tort' theory, and that OCGA § 9-3-33.1 (d)(1) validly revives her time-barred claims and is constitutional.
defendant_argument: The Harveys argued Merchan's claims were time-barred and not revivable under OCGA § 9-3-33.1 (d)(1) because the alleged acts did not meet the statutory definition of 'childhood sexual abuse' (due to age or location), and that the revival provision violated Georgia's constitutional ban on retroactive laws and federal and state due process and equal protection clauses.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and vacated in part, concluding that Georgia substantive law applies to torts committed in Georgia and Quebec substantive law to torts committed there, and remanded the case for the trial court to compare the respective limitations periods, while rejecting the Harveys' constitutional challenges.

title: Duke v. State
description: Whether an indigent defendant represented by private, pro bono counsel has a statutory or constitutional right to state-funded experts and investigators needed to prepare a defense.
plaintiff_argument: Duke argued that his indigent status entitles him to state-funded ancillary services under the Indigent Defense Act (IDA), and that his choice of pro bono counsel should not impede his constitutional right to due process and a fair trial by denying him these services.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Duke was no longer indigent under the IDA because he had pro bono counsel, that the IDA provides no mechanism for state funding for ancillary services for private counsel, and that Duke waived his constitutional right to such services by choosing private representation.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's ruling that pro bono counsel negates indigency and that the Indigent Defense Act provides no mechanism for state-funded ancillary services, vacating constitutional rulings and remanding the case for Duke to seek a contract for such services.
